title: What if a unit is split into four, twice?
description: A unit bar is split into four equal parts, and every part is split into four again. The tiny parts are counted by multiplying, then compared with splitting by ten twice and with the ten times rule of the places. Keeko's doubt is that the two fours are added.
teaching_notes: One idea: a second split multiplies the number of parts, and only a split by ten keeps every place ten times the next. Watch for students who add the two counts of four instead of multiplying them.

source: A unit is split into 4 equal parts, and each part is split i
video_script.why: The child has split a unit into ten parts and now sees what happens when the unit is split into four parts, twice.
video_script.substitution: A second split multiplies the number of parts, and a split by ten matches the ten times rule of the places.
video_script.anchor: a unit bar split into four equal parts, each part split into four again
video_script.wrong_move: adds the two counts of four instead of multiplying them
video_script.payoff_line: A unit then has sixteen tiny parts

final_answer.value: 16 parts of 1/16 each, against 100 parts of 1/100 each; 10 matches the 10 times rule of the places
final_answer.spoken: sixteen parts of one sixteenth each, against one hundred parts of one hundredth each

video_script.fraction_reading: one quarter, one sixteenth, one hundredth are said as words
hold_back: 16 parts of 1/16 each, against 100 parts of 1/100 each; 10 matches the 10 times rule of the places
maths_rules: first split: 4 equal parts, each 1/4 of a unit
second split: 4 quarters x 4 tiny parts = 4 x 4 = 16 tiny parts, each 1/16 of a unit
splitting by 10 twice: 10 x 10 = 100 parts, each 1/100 of a unit
in 281 each place is 10 times the place on its right: 10 ones = 1 ten, 10 tens = 1 hundred
the slip: 4 + 4 = 8 adds, but each of the 4 quarters holds its own 4 tiny parts
video_script.design: One unit bar all video; the quarters are split in the ground part, the counting and the comparison build in the working band, and Keeko's doubt strikes out the added count.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book, then a unit bar split into 4 equal parts with each part split into 4 again; a question mark in the anchor band

marks.split: the bar is split into 4 parts and every part into 4 again

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about splitting a unit.
<bookmark mark='split'/>A unit is split into four equal parts. Each part is split into four equal parts again.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many tiny parts make a unit? And how is that different from splitting by ten twice?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits beside it as the child
narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: one unit bar; it is cut into 4 equal parts, each 1/4; every quarter is then cut into 4 equal parts

marks.quarters: the bar is cut into 4 equal parts, each labelled 1/4
marks.again: every quarter is cut into 4 equal parts

narration: <bookmark mark='unit'/>Here is one unit, drawn as a bar.
<bookmark mark='quarters'/>The first split makes four equal parts, and each part is one quarter of the unit.
<bookmark mark='again'/>Next we cut every quarter into four equal parts again.

beats.on_screen: Given: a unit is split into 4 equal parts, and each part into 4 equal parts again
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a unit is split into four equal parts. Each part is split into four equal parts again.

beats.on_screen: To find: the number of tiny parts in a unit, and how this differs from splitting by 10 twice
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how many tiny parts make a unit. We also compare this with splitting by ten twice.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 4 quarters, each with 4 tiny parts, so the unit has 4 x 4 tiny parts

marks.count: 4 groups of 4 tiny parts are circled

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step one, count the tiny parts. Each of the four quarters holds four tiny parts.
<bookmark mark='mul'/>Four groups of four means we multiply four by four.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: splitting by 10 twice: 10 tenths, each cut into 10, so 10 x 10 parts; each part is 1/100 of a unit

marks.ten: a second bar is split into 10 parts, then each part into 10

narration: <bookmark mark='ten'/>Step two, split a unit by ten twice. Ten tenths, and each tenth is cut into ten more.
<bookmark mark='mul'/>That is ten groups of ten. We multiply ten by ten and get one hundred parts, each one hundredth.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: in 281 each place is 10 times the place on its right: 10 ones = 1 ten, 10 tens = 1 hundred; a split by 10 keeps this rule

marks.places: the places of 281 light up with arrows of 10 times
marks.why: ten ones and ten tens are grouped
marks.rule: the rule continues to the right of the ones

narration: <bookmark mark='places'/>Step three, look at the number two eight one. Each place is ten times the place on its right.
<bookmark mark='why'/>That is because ten ones make one ten and ten tens make one hundred.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Splitting a unit into ten parts keeps this same rule going to the right of the ones.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 16 parts of 1/16 each, against 100 parts of 1/100 each; 10 matches the 10 times rule of the places

marks.ten: the comparison with ten is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>A unit then has sixteen tiny parts, each one sixteenth of a unit.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>Splitting by ten twice gives one hundred parts, each one hundredth. Only ten matches the ten times rule of the places.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the unit bar
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: 4 + 4 = 8 appears and is struck out; the 4 quarters each show their own 4 tiny parts; 4 x 4 is written

marks.fix: each quarter shows its own 4 tiny parts and the sum is struck out

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks a unit has eight tiny parts, because four and four make eight.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But each of the four quarters holds four tiny parts of its own. That is four groups of four, so we multiply. The unit has sixteen tiny parts.
